claim: Human DNA2 (hDNA2) contains both a helicase and a nuclease domain within the same polypeptide.
source: Human DNA2 (hDNA2) contains both a helicase and a nuclease domain within the same polypeptide.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is a structural description of the protein.

claim: The nuclease of hDNA2 is involved in a variety of DNA metabolic processes.
source: The nuclease of hDNA2 is involved in a variety of DNA metabolic processes.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract referencing established knowledge about hDNA2 function.

claim: Little is known about the role of the hDNA2 helicase.
source: Little is known about the role of the hDNA2 helicase.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: hDNA2 is a processive helicase capable of unwinding kilobases of dsDNA in length.
source: Using bulk and single-molecule approaches, we show that hDNA2 is a processive helicase capable of unwinding kilobases of dsDNA in length.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from bulk and single-molecule assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: The nuclease activity prevents the engagement of the helicase by competing for the same substrate.
source: The nuclease activity prevents the engagement of the helicase by competing for the same substrate, hence prominent DNA unwinding by hDNA2 alone can only be observed using the nuclease-deficient variant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations comparing wild-type and nuclease-deficient variants.

claim: Prominent DNA unwinding by hDNA2 alone can only be observed using the nuclease-deficient variant.
source: The nuclease activity prevents the engagement of the helicase by competing for the same substrate, hence prominent DNA unwinding by hDNA2 alone can only be observed using the nuclease-deficient variant.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing DNA unwinding activity only with the D277A nuclease-deficient variant.

claim: The helicase of hDNA2 functionally integrates with BLM or WRN helicases to promote dsDNA degradation by forming a heterodimeric molecular machine.
source: We show that the helicase of hDNA2 functionally integrates with BLM or WRN helicases to promote dsDNA degradation by forming a heterodimeric molecular machine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing synergistic effects when hDNA2 is combined with BLM or WRN.

claim: The hDNA2 motor promotes the enzyme's capacity to degrade dsDNA in conjunction with BLM or WRN and thus promote the repair of broken DNA.
source: This collectively suggests that the hDNA2 motor promotes the enzyme's capacity to degrade dsDNA in conjunction with BLM or WRN and thus promote the repair of broken DNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and their biological context.

claim: DNA2 is an enzyme that contains both helicase and nuclease domains within the same polypeptide.
source: The DNA replication ATP-dependent helicase/nuclease 2 (DNA2) is an enzyme that contains both helicase and nuclease domains within the same polypeptide (Bae et al., 1998), and has important functions in a variety of DNA metabolic processes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: DNA2 has important functions in a variety of DNA metabolic processes.
source: The DNA replication ATP-dependent helicase/nuclease 2 (DNA2) is an enzyme that contains both helicase and nuclease domains within the same polypeptide (Bae et al., 1998), and has important functions in a variety of DNA metabolic processes.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the literature.

claim: Dna2 was first described in Saccharomyces cerevisiae where it is required for DNA replication under unperturbed conditions.
source: Dna2 was first described in Saccharomyces cerevisiae where it is required for DNA replication under unperturbed conditions (Budd and Campbell, 1995; Kuo et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During Okazaki fragment processing, yeast Dna2 (yDna2) cleaves long 5'-flaps that are coated by the Replication Protein A (RPA) and are therefore refractory to cleavage by Rad27 (FEN1).
source: Specifically, during Okazaki fragment processing, yeast Dna2 (yDna2) cleaves long 5'-flaps that are coated by the Replication Protein A (RPA) and are therefore refractory to cleavage by Rad27 (FEN1) (Bae et al., 2001; Levikova and Cejka, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: yDna2 is one of the nucleases that resect 5'-terminated strands of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: Moreover, yDna2 is one of the nucleases that resect 5'-terminated strands of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) (Cejka et al., 2010; Niu et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DNA end resection leads to the formation of 3'-tailed DNA, which becomes a substrate for the strand exchange protein Rad51 to initiate homology search and accurate DSB repair by the recombination machinery.
source: This process leads to the formation of 3'-tailed DNA, which becomes a substrate for the strand exchange protein Rad51 to initiate homology search and accurate DSB repair by the recombination machinery (Cejka, 2015; Heyer et al., 2010; Symington, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies describing the homologous recombination pathway.

claim: Yeast Dna2 functions upon replication stress to degrade structures such as reversed replication forks.
source: Yeast Dna2 also functions upon replication stress to degrades structures such as reversed replication forks (Hu et al., 2012; Thangavel et al., 2015) and has a structural role in DNA damage signaling, where it is a component in one out of three signaling branches that activate the Mec1 kinase in response to ssDNA in S-phase (Kumar and Burgers, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast Dna2 has a structural role in DNA damage signaling, where it is a component in one out of three signaling branches that activate the Mec1 kinase in response to ssDNA in S-phase.
source: Yeast Dna2 also functions upon replication stress to degrades structures such as reversed replication forks (Hu et al., 2012; Thangavel et al., 2015) and has a structural role in DNA damage signaling, where it is a component in one out of three signaling branches that activate the Mec1 kinase in response to ssDNA in S-phase (Kumar and Burgers, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: yDna2 was described to be required for the proper function of telomeres.
source: Additionally, yDna2 was described to be required for the proper function of telomeres (Choe et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The yeast Dna2 protein contains a large unstructured N-terminal domain, which mediates a physical interaction with yRPA.
source: The yeast Dna2 protein contains a large unstructured N-terminal domain, which mediates a physical interaction with yRPA (Bae et al., 2003), is required for Dna2's checkpoint function (Kumar and Burgers, 2013) and its capacity to melt secondary structures within 5' DNA flaps (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The N-terminal domain of yeast Dna2 is required for Dna2's checkpoint function.
source: The yeast Dna2 protein contains a large unstructured N-terminal domain, which mediates a physical interaction with yRPA (Bae et al., 2003), is required for Dna2's checkpoint function (Kumar and Burgers, 2013) and its capacity to melt secondary structures within 5' DNA flaps (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The N-terminal domain of yeast Dna2 is required for its capacity to melt secondary structures within 5' DNA flaps.
source: The yeast Dna2 protein contains a large unstructured N-terminal domain, which mediates a physical interaction with yRPA (Bae et al., 2003), is required for Dna2's checkpoint function (Kumar and Burgers, 2013) and its capacity to melt secondary structures within 5' DNA flaps (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The N-terminal domain of yeast Dna2 is followed by a RecB-like nuclease domain.
source: The N-terminal domain is followed by a RecB-like nuclease domain (Budd et al., 2000) and a Superfamily I helicase domain in the C-terminal part of the polypeptide (Budd and Campbell, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies describing the domain structure.

claim: Yeast Dna2 contains a Superfamily I helicase domain in the C-terminal part of the polypeptide.
source: The N-terminal domain is followed by a RecB-like nuclease domain (Budd et al., 2000) and a Superfamily I helicase domain in the C-terminal part of the polypeptide (Budd and Campbell, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: With the exception of checkpoint signaling, all Dna2 functions are exclusively dependent on its nuclease activity.
source: With the exception of checkpoint signaling, all Dna2 functions are exclusively dependent on its nuclease activity (Sturzenegger et al., 2014; Thangavel et al., 2015; Wanrooij and Burgers, 2015; Zhu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dna2 homologs are present in all eukaryotic organisms including human cells.
source: Dna2 homologs are present in all eukaryotic organisms including human cells (Budd and Campbell, 1995; Eki et al., 1996; Gould et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both helicase and nuclease domains are well conserved in evolution, but the unstructured N-terminal domain is only present in lower eukaryotes.
source: Both helicase and nuclease domains are well conserved in evolution, but the unstructured N-terminal domain is only present in lower eukaryotes (Bae et al., 1998; Kang et al., 2010; Wanrooij and Burgers, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human DNA2 (hDNA2) functions in DNA end resection.
source: Human DNA2 (hDNA2) also functions in DNA end resection (Gravel et al., 2008; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Sturzenegger et al., 2014) and in the processing of non-canonical DNA replication structures, such as reversed replication forks upon replication stress (Duxin et al., 2012; Thangavel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: hDNA2 functions in the processing of non-canonical DNA replication structures, such as reversed replication forks upon replication stress.
source: Human DNA2 (hDNA2) also functions in DNA end resection (Gravel et al., 2008; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Sturzenegger et al., 2014) and in the processing of non-canonical DNA replication structures, such as reversed replication forks upon replication stress (Duxin et al., 2012; Thangavel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In contrast to yeast, hDNA2 appears to be dispensable for the processing of most Okazaki fragments.
source: In contrast to yeast, however, hDNA2 appears to be dispensable for the processing of most Okazaki fragments (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Specific inactivation of the nuclease, as well as the depletion or knockout of the protein/gene, result in lethal phenotypes in all organisms tested to date.
source: Specific inactivation of the nuclease, as well as the depletion or knockout of the protein/gene, result in lethal phenotypes in all organisms tested to date (Budd et al., 2000; Duxin et al., 2012; Kang et al., 2000; Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In yeast, the lethality of Dna2 inactivation has been ascribed to yDna2's role in Okazaki fragment processing.
source: In yeast, this has been ascribed to yDna2's role in Okazaki fragment processing (Kang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Human DNA2-depleted cells arrest at late S/G2 phase of the cell cycle.
source: Human DNA2-depleted cells arrest at late S/G2 phase of the cell cycle (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The lethality of hDNA2-depleted cells may result from the failure to process reversed replication forks or other aberrant structures that arise during replication stress.
source: It is conceivable that the lethality of hDNA2-depleted cells results from the failure to process reversed replication forks or other aberrant structures that arise during replication stress even in the absence of treatment with genotoxic drugs (Duxin et al., 2012; Thangavel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited studies.

claim: The role of hDNA2 in DSB end resection does not appear to be essential for viability as it functions redundantly with another nuclease, Exonuclease 1 (EXO1).
source: The role of hDNA2 in DSB end resection in contrast does not appear to be essential for viability as it functions redundantly with another nuclease, Exonuclease 1 (EXO1) (Gravel et al., 2008; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Tomimatsu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EXO1 is not involved in the processing of reversed replication forks.
source: EXO1 is not involved in the processing of reversed replication forks, pointing towards an essential function of hDNA2 in the response to intermediates arising during DNA replication (Thangavel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The nuclease of hDNA2 is specific for ssDNA.
source: The nuclease of hDNA2 is specific for ssDNA (Kim et al., 2006; Masuda-Sasa et al., 2006) and therefore requires an associated helicase activity to resect/degrade dsDNA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The nuclease of hDNA2 requires an associated helicase activity to resect/degrade dsDNA.
source: The nuclease of hDNA2 is specific for ssDNA (Kim et al., 2006; Masuda-Sasa et al., 2006) and therefore requires an associated helicase activity to resect/degrade dsDNA.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the ssDNA specificity of the nuclease.

claim: BLM or WRN serve as helicase partners for hDNA2 during DSB end resection.
source: This was shown to be either BLM or WRN during DSB end resection (Gravel et al., 2008; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Sturzenegger et al., 2014), or primarily WRN to degrade non-canonical DNA structures arising during DNA replication (Thangavel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: WRN primarily serves as the helicase partner for hDNA2 to degrade non-canonical DNA structures arising during DNA replication.
source: This was shown to be either BLM or WRN during DSB end resection (Gravel et al., 2008; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Sturzenegger et al., 2014), or primarily WRN to degrade non-canonical DNA structures arising during DNA replication (Thangavel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The inherent helicase of hDNA2 was not required for DSB end resection or processing of replication structures.
source: Interestingly, the inherent helicase of hDNA2 was not required for these processes (Sturzenegger et al., 2014; Thangavel et al., 2015), and the function of the hDNA2 motor activity remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The helicase function of yeast Dna2 is not essential for viability in yeast.
source: The helicase function is not essential for viability in yeast (Bae et al., 2002), where it was proposed to unwind secondary structures forming on long flaps at the 5' ends of Okazaki fragments (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The yeast Dna2 helicase was proposed to unwind secondary structures forming on long flaps at the 5' ends of Okazaki fragments.
source: The helicase function is not essential for viability in yeast (Bae et al., 2002), where it was proposed to unwind secondary structures forming on long flaps at the 5' ends of Okazaki fragments (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Yeast dna2 cells lacking the helicase activity are dramatically sensitive to alkylating agents such as methyl methanesulfonate (MMS).
source: Yeast dna2 cells lacking the helicase activity are dramatically sensitive to alkylating agents such as methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) (Budd and Campbell, 1995), suggesting that the yDna2 helicase might also play a role in the response to replication stress.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Both helicase and nuclease functions are essential for viability in human cells.
source: In contrast to yeast, both helicase and nuclease functions are essential for viability in human cells (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: hDNA2 helicase-deficient cells exhibit a terminal S/G2 cell cycle arrest.
source: Similarly to hDNA2 nuclease-deficient cells, hDNA2 helicase-deficient cells also exhibit a terminal S/G2 cell cycle arrest, most likely due to the inability to resolve structures arising in S-phase (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: hDNA2 nuclease-deficient cells displayed cell cycle defects that were even more severe than upon depletion of hDNA2.
source: Furthermore, hDNA2 nuclease-deficient cells displayed cell cycle defects that were even more severe than upon depletion of hDNA2; interestingly, this phenotype was dependent on the integrity of the Walker A motif within the helicase domain (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The severe phenotype of hDNA2 nuclease-deficient cells was dependent on the integrity of the Walker A motif within the helicase domain.
source: Furthermore, hDNA2 nuclease-deficient cells displayed cell cycle defects that were even more severe than upon depletion of hDNA2; interestingly, this phenotype was dependent on the integrity of the Walker A motif within the helicase domain (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The hDNA2 helicase performs essential functions during DNA replication, yet it becomes toxic in the absence of the nuclease.
source: This suggested that the hDNA2 helicase performs essential functions during DNA replication, yet it becomes toxic in the absence of the nuclease (Duxin et al., 2012), although mechanistic insights into the interplay between both activities have been lacking.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on a cited study.

claim: One work concluded that hDNA2 lacks a helicase activity.
source: One work concluded that hDNA2 lacks a helicase activity (Kim et al., 2006), whereas another study could detect DNA unwinding, albeit very weak and distributive (Masuda-Sasa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Another study could detect DNA unwinding by hDNA2, albeit very weak and distributive.
source: One work concluded that hDNA2 lacks a helicase activity (Kim et al., 2006), whereas another study could detect DNA unwinding, albeit very weak and distributive (Masuda-Sasa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: It has been proposed that the helicase domain may be more responsible for DNA binding rather than as a motor activity per se.
source: It has been also proposed that the helicase domain may be more responsible for DNA binding rather than as a motor activity per se (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The sequence of hDNA2 was codon-optimized for the expression in Spodoptera frugiperda 9 (Sf9) cells, which improved the yield ~2–3 fold.
source: The sequence of hDNA2 was codon-optimized (Supplementary file 1A) for the expression in Spodoptera frugiperda 9 (Sf9) cells, which improved the yield ~2–3 fold (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations during protein expression.

claim: hDNA2 contains an iron-sulfur cluster.
source: Considering that hDNA2 contains an iron-sulfur cluster (Pokharel and Campbell, 2012; Yeeles et al., 2009), all buffers were degassed and contained reducing agents throughout the preparation procedure to prevent oxidation of the cluster, as described previously for S. cerevisiae Dna2 (Levikova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Wild type hDNA2, nuclease-deficient D277A, helicase-deficient K654R as well as nuclease- and helicase-deficient D277A K654R variants were purified to near homogeneity.
source: Wild type hDNA2, nuclease-deficient D277A, helicase-deficient K654R as well as nuclease- and helicase-deficient D277A K654R variants were purified in the same manner to near homogeneity (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the protein purification gels shown in the figures.

claim: The yield of the recombinant proteins was ~330–390 μg from 3 liters of Sf9 cell culture except for the variant containing the K654R mutation, which yielded only ~27 μg.
source: The yield of the recombinant proteins was ~330–390 μg from 3 liters of Sf9 cell culture except for the variant containing the K654R mutation, which yielded only ~27 μg.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of protein yield.

claim: Without hRPA, hDNA2 most efficiently degraded ssDNA, while 5'-overhanged, 3'-overhanged and Y-structured DNA were degraded ~7–20-fold less efficiently.
source: Without the human Replication Protein A (hRPA), hDNA2 most efficiently degraded ssDNA, while 5'-overhanged, 3'-overhanged and Y-structured DNA were degraded ~7–20-fold less efficiently, based on the hDNA2 concentration required for the degradation of 50% DNA substrate (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of nuclease assays shown in the figures.

claim: dsDNA was largely refractory to cleavage by hDNA2 without hRPA.
source: In contrast, dsDNA was largely refractory to cleavage (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), in agreement with the observations that hDNA2 needs a helicase partner in DNA end resection to initiate homologous recombination (Cejka et al., 2010; Gravel et al., 2008; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Sturzenegger et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and is consistent with cited studies.

claim: The helicase-deficient hDNA2 (K654R) variant displayed a nuclease activity indistinguishable from that of the wild type enzyme on a 5'-tailed DNA substrate.
source: As reported previously (Masuda-Sasa et al., 2006), the helicase-deficient hDNA2 (K654R) variant displayed a nuclease activity indistinguishable from that of the wild type enzyme on a 5'-tailed DNA substrate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and is consistent with a cited study.

claim: hRPA directs the nuclease of hDNA2 towards the 5' terminus while inhibiting the 3'-5' nuclease activity.
source: Using a 3'-end labeled ssDNA, we observed that hRPA directs the nuclease of hDNA2 towards the 5' terminus; while at the same time inhibits the 3'-5' nuclease activity (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data using 3'-end labeled DNA.

claim: hRPA enforces the correct polarity of DNA degradation during DNA end resection.
source: This is in agreement with previous observations in various organisms (Cejka et al., 2010; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2015) and explains how hRPA enforces the correct polarity of DNA degradation during DNA end resection.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental data and cited studies.

claim: In the presence of hRPA, hDNA2 most efficiently cleaved Y-structured and 5'-tailed DNA substrates, which were degraded ~5–10-fold more efficiently than ssDNA.
source: Interestingly, in the presence of hRPA, hDNA2 most efficiently cleaved Y-structured and 5'-tailed DNA substrates, which were degraded ~5–10-fold more efficiently than ssDNA (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of nuclease assays shown in the figures.

claim: The nuclease activities of yeast Dna2 and human DNA2 are very similar qualitatively, but human DNA2 appears somewhat less active (~2-fold in degradation of 5'-tailed DNA) than its yeast homologue.
source: In summary, the nuclease activities of yeast Dna2 and human DNA2 are very similar qualitatively, but human DNA2 appears somewhat less active (~2-fold in degradation of 5'-tailed DNA) than its yeast homologue (Levikova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data with a cited study.

claim: hDNA2 D277A strongly bound ssDNA, with KD ~2 nM for ssDNA of 50 nucleotides in length.
source: hDNA2 D277A strongly bound ssDNA, with KD ~2 nM for ssDNA of 50 nucleotides in length (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is based on DNA binding assays shown in the figures.

claim: Similar binding affinity was observed for Y-structured DNA, while the apparent DNA binding to 5' and 3'-tailed structures was reduced ~8–12-fold, respectively, compared to ssDNA.
source: Similar binding affinity was observed for Y-structured DNA, while the apparent DNA binding to 5' and 3'-tailed structures was reduced ~8–12-fold, respectively, compared to ssDNA.
evidence: This is based on DNA binding assays.

claim: dsDNA was bound very poorly by hDNA2 D277A.
source: In contrast, dsDNA was bound very poorly (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is based on DNA binding assays shown in the figures.

claim: The DNA binding affinity was determined by the length of ssDNA rather than the specific structure.
source: Further experiments revealed that the DNA binding affinity was determined by the length of ssDNA rather than the specific structure (Figure 1H,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: This is based on DNA binding assays with substrates of varying lengths.

claim: hDNA2 exhibits a preference for DNA structures with a free 5' end.
source: Remarkably, the distinct DNA-protein species that entered the polyacrylamide gel were only observed with substrates containing a free 5' end such as Y-structured, 5' tailed or ssDNA substrates (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,F), suggesting that hDNA2 exhibits a preference for this structure even in the absence of hRPA.
evidence: This is based on DNA binding assays showing distinct migration patterns.

claim: hDNA2 hydrolyses ATP.
source: Previous reports concluded that hDNA2 hydrolyses ATP, as expected from a protein containing an SFI helicase domain (Budd and Campbell, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The ATPase activity of hDNA2 D277A was strongly enhanced in the presence of DNA cofactors.
source: We next determined the ATP hydrolysis rate of nuclease-deficient hDNA2 D277A in the presence of various DNA structures. The ATPase activity was strongly enhanced in the presence the DNA cofactors.
evidence: This is based on ATPase assays with various DNA substrates.

claim: The greatest stimulation of ATPase activity, ~13-fold, was observed with 5'-tailed DNA.
source: The greatest stimulation, ~13-fold, was observed with 5'-tailed DNA (Figure 2A), in agreement with the 5'-3' polarity of the hDNA2 helicase (Balakrishnan et al., 2010a; Balakrishnan et al., 2010b; Masuda-Sasa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on ATPase assays and is consistent with cited studies.

claim: The apparent turnover rate (kcat) of the ATP hydrolysis in the presence of 5'-tailed substrates of different lengths was 6.9 ± 1.1 s−1 and 6.2 ± 0.9 s−1.
source: The apparent turnover rate (kcat) of the ATP hydrolysis in the presence of 5'-tailed substrates of different lengths was 6.9 ± 1.1 s−1 and 6.2 ± 0.9 s−1.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of ATPase assays.

claim: dsDNA stimulated the hDNA2 ATPase to the lowest extent, ~four-fold, compared to reactions without DNA.
source: In contrast, dsDNA stimulated the hDNA2 ATPase to the lowest extent, ~four-fold, compared to reactions without DNA.
evidence: This is based on ATPase assays with dsDNA.

claim: The ATP hydrolysis rate increased with poly(dT) concentration, with Vmax = 3.1 ± 0.3 μM·min−1 and KM = 115 ± 45 nM (in nucleotides).
source: As expected, the ATP hydrolysis rate increased with poly(dT) concentration. The measured reaction rate values were fitted into a Michaelis-Menten curve with Vmax = 3.1 ± 0.3 μM·min−1 and KM = 115 ± 45 nM (in nucleotides, Figure 2B), which corresponds to kcat = 4.3 ± 0.4 s−1.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of ATPase assays with varying poly(dT) concentrations.

claim: The rate of ATP hydrolysis by the nuclease-deficient D277A variant incubated with 5'-tailed substrate was constant over time.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 2C, the rate of ATP hydrolysis by the nuclease-deficient D277A variant incubated with 5'-tailed substrate was constant over time.
evidence: This is based on time-course ATPase assays shown in the figure.

claim: The rate of ATP consumption decreased quickly in case of wild type DNA2.
source: In contrast the rate of ATP consumption decreased quickly in case of wild type DNA2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on time-course ATPase assays shown in the figure.

claim: The nuclease activity of hDNA2 rapidly degrades the 5' ssDNA overhang, producing a substrate that is less efficient as a cofactor for the ATPase activity.
source: We believe that the nuclease activity of hDNA2 rapidly degrades the 5' ssDNA overhang, producing a substrate that is less efficient as a cofactor for the ATPase activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The ATPase activity of hDNA2 qualitatively resembles that of the yeast Dna2 homologue in terms of DNA substrate preference and interplay with the nuclease activity, but it is ~10-fold less active in quantitative terms.
source: Collectively, these experiments establish that the ATPase activity of hDNA2 qualitatively resembles that of the yeast Dna2 homologue in terms of DNA substrate preference and interplay with the nuclease activity, but it is ~10-fold less active in quantitative terms (Levikova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data with a cited study.

claim: The capacity to unwind DNA by human DNA2 has been controversial.
source: The capacity to unwind DNA by human DNA2 has been controversial. Previously, hDNA2's helicase activity was either described as undetectable (Kim et al., 2006) or very weak (Balakrishnan et al., 2010a; Masuda-Sasa et al., 2006), capable to unwind only short duplexes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies with conflicting results.

claim: S. cerevisiae Dna2 possesses a vigorous and processive helicase activity that is masked by its nuclease activity.
source: In our earlier studies, we could show that S. cerevisiae Dna2 possesses a vigorous and processive helicase activity that is masked by its nuclease activity (Levikova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: hDNA2 D277A efficiently unwound dsDNA fragments of up to 2.3 kbp in length.
source: Figure 3A and B demonstrate that hDNA2 D277A efficiently unwound dsDNA fragments of up to 2.3 kbp in length, whereas unwinding of ≥9.4 kbp-long fragments was barely detectable within the 30 min incubation time.
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: Unwinding of ≥9.4 kbp-long fragments was barely detectable within the 30 min incubation time.
source: Figure 3A and B demonstrate that hDNA2 D277A efficiently unwound dsDNA fragments of up to 2.3 kbp in length, whereas unwinding of ≥9.4 kbp-long fragments was barely detectable within the 30 min incubation time.
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: Unwinding of long DNA molecules was evident in kinetic experiments upon longer incubation times.
source: Unwinding of these long DNA molecules was however evident in kinetic experiments upon longer incubation times (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on time-course helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: The dsDNA unwinding capacity of hDNA2 D277A was fully dependent on hRPA and ATP.
source: This unexpected dsDNA unwinding capacity of hDNA2 D277A was fully dependent on hRPA and ATP (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays with and without hRPA and ATP.

claim: The nuclease-deficient hDNA2 D277A variant unwound a 2.7 kbp-long plasmid-based dsDNA substrate in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: The nuclease-deficient hDNA2 D277A variant also similarly unwound a 2.7 kbp-long plasmid-based dsDNA substrate in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: The nuclease- and helicase-deficient DNA2 D277A K654R mutant did not unwind DNA.
source: In contrast, the nuclease- and helicase-deficient DNA2 D277A K654R mutant did not unwind DNA, as expected, showing that the unwinding capacity is inherent to the helicase activity of hDNA2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays with the double mutant shown in the figure.

claim: The Y-structure was unwound most efficiently by hDNA2 D277A.
source: We found that the Y-structure was unwound most efficiently (Figure 3F,G), followed by the 5' overhang (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays with various DNA substrates shown in the figures.

claim: No DNA unwinding was observed with 3' overhang and dsDNA.
source: In contrast, no DNA unwinding was observed with 3' overhang and dsDNA (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E), in agreement with the 5'-3' polarity of DNA unwinding by hDNA2 and its homologues (Bae et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures and is consistent with cited studies.

claim: No dsDNA unwinding was observed with wild type hDNA2.
source: Importantly, no dsDNA unwinding was observed with wild type hDNA2 (Figure 3A, lane 9).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figure.

claim: The hDNA2 nuclease is efficient in ssDNA degradation at sub-nanomolar concentrations.
source: The hDNA2 nuclease is efficient in ssDNA degradation at sub-nanomolar concentrations (Figure 1E), and thus likely degrades the 5' ssDNA overhangs that are required for the initiation of DNA unwinding.
evidence: This is based on nuclease assays shown in the figure.

claim: By degrading 5'-tailed DNA the nuclease of hDNA2 masks the helicase capacity of the wild type polypeptide.
source: By degrading 5'-tailed DNA the nuclease of hDNA2 masks the helicase capacity of the wild type polypeptide, similarly as in yeast (Levikova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental data and is consistent with a cited study.

claim: The nuclease of DNA2 is situated ahead of the helicase domain, and therefore has the capacity to degrade 5'-terminated ssDNA tails to prevent DNA loading of the helicase domain.
source: This is in agreement with a recent structural study, which determined that the nuclease of DNA2 is situated ahead of the helicase domain, and therefore has the capacity to degrade 5'-terminated ssDNA tails to prevent DNA loading of the helicase domain (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a structural study.

claim: The inactivation of the hDNA2 nuclease unleashes the hDNA2 helicase likely provides explanation for the pronounced toxicity of a nuclease-deficient hDNA2 construct in vivo.
source: Our observation that the inactivation of the hDNA2 nuclease unleashes the hDNA2 helicase likely provides explanation for the pronounced toxicity of a nuclease-deficient hDNA2 construct in vivo, which was dependent on the integrity of the Walker A motif within hDNA2 (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental findings and a cited study.

claim: Nuclease-deficient hDNA2 possesses the capacity to unwind dsDNA of kilobases in length in a reaction dependent on hRPA and ATP.
source: In summary, we show that nuclease-deficient hDNA2 possesses the capacity to unwind dsDNA of kilobases in length in a reaction dependent on hRPA and ATP.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Wild type hDNA2 is devoid of any apparent dsDNA unwinding activity.
source: Wild type hDNA2 is devoid of any apparent dsDNA unwinding activity, which likely infers the existence of mechanisms that allow the manifestation of the motor activity in the context of the wild type polypeptide under specific conditions.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and speculation about regulatory mechanisms.

claim: hDNA2 D277A can unwind long stretches of dsDNA.
source: DNA unwinding experiment with λDNA (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) showed that hDNA2 D277A can unwind long stretches of dsDNA.
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: DNA2 cannot unwind DNA from internal sites and can only initiate from a free DNA end.
source: As DNA2 cannot unwind DNA from internal sites and can only initiate from a free DNA end (Balakrishnan et al., 2010a; Zhou et al., 2015), we used a 20-fold excess of each helicase over the substrate to saturate the DNA ends.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ssDNA was detected after only one minute of the reaction with the yeast enzyme, whereas it took eight minutes to detect a similar amount of unwound DNA for the human DNA2 variant.
source: We detected ssDNA after only one minute of the reaction with the yeast enzyme, whereas it took eight minutes to detect a similar amount of unwound DNA for the human DNA2 variant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is based on kinetic helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: hDNA2 unwound the dsDNA substrate slowly but consecutively over time.
source: We observed that hDNA2 unwound the dsDNA substrate slowly but consecutively over time (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on single-molecule magnetic tweezers experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Most of the DNA molecules underwent significant dsDNA unwinding of several kilobases in length, with some molecules showing unwinding of the full-length 6.1 kbp substrate.
source: Most of the DNA molecules underwent significant dsDNA unwinding of several kilobases in length, with some molecules showing unwinding of the full-length 6.1 kbp substrate.
evidence: This is based on single-molecule magnetic tweezers experiments.

claim: The unwinding rates were broadly distributed between 0 to 40 bp/s.
source: The unwinding rates were broadly distributed between 0 to 40 bp/s.
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-molecule unwinding trajectories.

claim: The distribution had a pronounced maximum at around 10 bp⋅s−1 and the mean unwinding rate was 12.8 ± 0.8 bp⋅s−1.
source: The distribution had a pronounced maximum at around 10 bp⋅s−1 and the mean unwinding rate was 12.8 ± 0.8 bp⋅s−1, which is ~3-fold slower than that of the yeast homologue (Levikova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of single-molecule unwinding rates and comparison with a cited study.

claim: Long-range processive dsDNA unwinding was dependent on ATP and hRPA.
source: Long-range processive dsDNA unwinding was dependent on ATP and hRPA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D), in agreement with the experiments shown above.
evidence: This is based on single-molecule experiments shown in the figures.

claim: DNA unwinding continued despite successive washing steps, indicating that the originally acting unwinding complex remained bound and active during the course of the observation period.
source: DNA unwinding continued despite successive washing steps, indicating that the originally acting unwinding complex remained bound and active during the course of the observation period.
evidence: This is based on single-molecule experiments with buffer washing.

claim: The DNA2 D277A helicase is highly processive.
source: This demonstrated that the DNA2 D277A helicase is highly processive (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on single-molecule experiments shown in the figure.

claim: ssDNA must feed through a narrow tunnel to reach the helicase domain.
source: The recently-published structure of DNA2 shows that ssDNA must feed through a narrow tunnel to reach the helicase domain (Zhou et al., 2015), which likely prevents dissociation of DNA2 from its substrate and corroborates the high processivity observed in our assays.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a structural study and is used to explain the observed processivity.

claim: No direction reversals during unwinding (i.e. rezipping) that could originate from strand–switches were observed.
source: In agreement with this no direction reversals during unwinding (i.e. rezipping) that could originate from strand–switches were observed (Dessinges et al., 2004; Klaue et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-molecule unwinding trajectories and is consistent with cited studies.

claim: The hRPA protein is a critical cofactor of the hDNA2 nuclease as well as the helicase activities.
source: The hRPA protein is a critical cofactor of the hDNA2 nuclease (Figure 1) as well as the helicase activities (Figure 3) (Nimonkar et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figures and is consistent with cited studies.

claim: hDNA2 was initially described as a mitochondrial protein before its function in nuclear DNA metabolism was determined.
source: Initially, hDNA2 was described as a mitochondrial protein (Zheng et al., 2008) before its function in nuclear DNA metabolism was determined (Duxin et al., 2009; Gravel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mitochondria contain the mitochondrial single-stranded DNA binding protein (mtSSB), a homotetramer similar to the SSB protein of Escherichia coli.
source: Mitochondria are devoid of hRPA; instead, they contain the mitochondrial single-stranded DNA binding protein (mtSSB), a homotetramer similar to the SSB protein of Escherichia coli (Curth et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The sensor of single-stranded DNA (SOSS) complex was described in the nucleus of human cells.
source: Furthermore, the sensor of single-stranded DNA (SOSS) complex was described in the nucleus of human cells (Huang et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SOSS likely regulates various aspects of DNA metabolism including DNA recombination and DNA end resection by the MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 (MRN) complex and EXO1.
source: SOSS likely regulates various aspects of DNA metabolism including DNA recombination and DNA end resection by the MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 (MRN) complex and EXO1 (Richard et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neither mtSSB nor SOSS were able to substitute hRPA to promote dsDNA unwinding by hDNA2 D277A.
source: Neither mtSSB (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) nor SOSS (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) were able to substitute hRPA to promote dsDNA unwinding.
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: The hDNA2-hRPA functional interaction was largely species-specific, as yRPA from S. cerevisiae promoted DNA unwinding to a much lesser extent than the cognate hRPA.
source: The hDNA2-hRPA functional interaction was largely species-specific, as yRPA from S. cerevisiae promoted DNA unwinding to a much lesser extent than the cognate hRPA (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: hRPA is a unique and an essential co-factor of the hDNA2 helicase, which is required for the unwinding of all DNA duplex substrate lengths tested.
source: Therefore, hRPA is a unique and an essential co-factor of the hDNA2 helicase, which is required for the unwinding of all DNA duplex substrate lengths tested.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: hRPA could be replaced by yRPA in ssDNA degradation, which similarly directed the nuclease activity of hDNA2 towards the 5' end of ssDNA.
source: In contrast to dsDNA unwinding, hRPA could be replaced by yRPA in ssDNA degradation, which similarly directed the nuclease activity of hDNA2 towards the 5' end of ssDNA (Figure 1D, Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on nuclease assays shown in the figures.

claim: A much weaker effect was observed in the presence of the SOSS complex in directing nuclease activity.
source: Similar, albeit much weaker effect was observed in the presence of the SOSS complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, lane 28), possibly due to a lower affinity of SOSS towards ssDNA compared to the RPA proteins.
evidence: This is based on nuclease assays shown in the figure.

claim: The mtSSB dramatically inhibited all nuclease activities of hDNA2.
source: Considering the postulated function of the hDNA2 nuclease in mitochondrial DNA metabolism, the mtSSB unexpectedly dramatically inhibited all nuclease activities of hDNA2 (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on nuclease assays shown in the figures.

claim: hDNA2 functions in conjunction with a helicase partner in DNA end resection.
source: It has been established that hDNA2 functions in conjunction with a helicase partner in DNA end resection.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: BLM was initially described as the cognate partner of hDNA2.
source: Initially, it has been described that the cognate partner is BLM (Gravel et al., 2008; Nimonkar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: WRN could function in a redundant manner instead of BLM, or even be the sole helicase partner of hDNA2 during resection of reversed replication forks.
source: Later, it was demonstrated that also WRN could function in a redundant manner instead of BLM, or even be the sole helicase partner of hDNA2 during resection of reversed replication forks (Sturzenegger et al., 2014; Thangavel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Wild type hDNA2 was more efficient in DNA degradation than its helicase-deficient variant, in particular together with the WRN helicase.
source: Furthermore, wild type hDNA2 was more efficient in DNA degradation than its helicase-deficient variant, in particular together with the WRN helicase (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is based on DNA resection assays shown in the figures.

claim: Both wild type and helicase-deficient hDNA2 variants had indistinguishable nuclease activity on 5'-labeled oligonucleotide based substrate.
source: As shown above, both wild type and helicase-deficient hDNA2 variants had indistinguishable nuclease activity on 5'-labeled oligonucleotide based substrate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is based on nuclease assays shown in the figures.

claim: dsDNA unwinding/degradation by the enzyme pair is up to six-fold higher than the sum of activities of the polypeptides acting individually.
source: This indicates a synergistic relationship between the two enzyme pairs, i.e. that dsDNA unwinding/degradation by the enzyme pair is up to six-fold higher than the sum of activities of the polypeptides acting individually (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of DNA resection assays shown in the figure.

claim: Adding hDNA2 to reactions together with RecQ1 or RecQ5 did not result in any enhancement of DNA degradation.
source: We did not observe any enhancement of DNA degradation by hDNA2 upon adding either RecQ1 or RecQ5 helicases (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on DNA resection assays shown in the figure.

claim: Adding hDNA2 to reactions together with Sgs1 resulted in the degradation of unwound ssDNA, but no additional double-stranded substrate was degraded.
source: Importantly, adding hDNA2 to reactions together with Sgs1 resulted in the degradation of unwound ssDNA, but in contrast to the reactions with BLM or WRN, no additional double-stranded substrate was degraded.
evidence: This is based on DNA resection assays.

claim: hDNA2 appeared to inhibit dsDNA unwinding by Sgs1.
source: Moreover, hDNA2 even appeared to inhibit dsDNA unwinding by Sgs1 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on DNA resection assays shown in the figure.

claim: The specific stimulatory effect was observed in kinetic experiments with BLM and WRN, while no stimulation was observed with hDNA2 and Sgs1.
source: The specific stimulatory effect was also observed in kinetic experiments with BLM and WRN, while no stimulation was observed with hDNA2 and Sgs1 (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: This is based on kinetic DNA resection assays shown in the figures.

claim: The stimulation of DNA degradation by hDNA2 was particularly pronounced together with WRN, where a gradual degradation of the substrate was observed.
source: The stimulation of DNA degradation by hDNA2 was particularly pronounced together with WRN, where a gradual degradation of the substrate was observed (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on kinetic DNA resection assays shown in the figure.

claim: The observed degradation pattern is indicative of a 5'-3' polarity of DNA degradation by hDNA2, and appears unrelated to the 3'-5' exonuclease of WRN on recessed 3' ends.
source: As our substrate is labeled on the 3' end, the observed degradation pattern is indicative of a 5'-3' polarity of DNA degradation by hDNA2, and appears unrelated to the 3'-5' exonuclease of WRN on recessed 3' ends (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental design and results.

claim: The hDNA2-BLM and hDNA2-WRN functionally integrate and the helicase of hDNA2 may have a stimulatory role in DNA end resection.
source: Together, these experiments show that the hDNA2-BLM and hDNA2-WRN functionally integrate and that the helicase of hDNA2 may have a stimulatory role in DNA end resection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Nuclease-deficient yDna2 E675A exhibits a very vigorous DNA helicase activity similar to the helicase of Sgs1.
source: Our previous work revealed that nuclease-deficient yDna2 E675A exhibits a very vigorous DNA helicase activity similar to the helicase of Sgs1, one of the most active helicases in eukaryotes (Cejka and Kowalczykowski, 2010; Levikova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Under elevated ionic strength conditions, the yDna2 E675A variant was even more active than Sgs1.
source: Interestingly, we found here that under elevated ionic strength conditions, the yDna2 E675A variant was even more active than Sgs1 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figure.

claim: DNA unwinding by hDNA2 D277A was highly sensitive to NaCl, to a much greater extent than dsDNA unwinding by BLM or WRN.
source: In contrast DNA unwinding by hDNA2 D277A was highly sensitive to NaCl, to a much greater extent than dsDNA unwinding by BLM or WRN (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays with varying salt concentrations shown in the figure.

claim: Helicase-deficient WRN K577M or BLM K695A stimulated the hDNA2 D277A helicase activity ~7 or ~4-fold, respectively.
source: Supplementing the reaction with WRN K577M or BLM K695A stimulated the hDNA2 D277A helicase activity ~7 or ~4-fold, respectively (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: Both BLM and WRN have structural roles to promote dsDNA unwinding by the nuclease-deficient hDNA2 D277A.
source: Therefore, both BLM and WRN have structural roles to promote dsDNA unwinding by the nuclease-deficient hDNA2 D277A.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: This stimulatory effect was specific for WRN and BLM helicases, as none of the other helicase-deficient enzymes tested stimulated DNA unwinding to a comparable extent.
source: This stimulatory effect was specific for WRN and BLM helicases, as none of the other helicase-deficient enzymes tested stimulated DNA unwinding to a comparable extent (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: Adding the hDNA2 D277A variant to dsDNA unwinding reactions containing wild type WRN resulted in an increase in DNA unwinding (~2.4-fold), which was more than upon the addition of the nuclease- and helicase-deficient hDNA2 D277A K654R variant (~1.5-fold stimulation).
source: Under the same conditions, we could observe that adding the hDNA2 D277A variant to dsDNA unwinding reactions containing wild type WRN resulted in an increase in DNA unwinding (~2.4-fold), which was more that upon the addition of the nuclease- and helicase-deficient hDNA2 D277A K654R variant (~1.5-fold stimulation, Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures.

claim: The hDNA2 helicase functionally integrates with WRN even under experimental conditions when no inherent helicase activity was detected.
source: Therefore, the hDNA2 helicase functionally integrates with WRN even under experimental conditions when no inherent helicase activity was detected.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: hDNA2 has only a structural role to promote dsDNA unwinding by wild type BLM, as both hDNA2 D277A and DNA2 D277A K654R variants stimulated DNA unwinding by BLM to the same extent.
source: In contrast, we observed that hDNA2 has only a structural role to promote dsDNA unwinding by wild type BLM, as both hDNA2 D277A and DNA2 D277A K654R variants stimulated DNA unwinding by BLM to the same extent (Figure 7G,H), as noted by Sung and colleagues previously (Daley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on helicase assays shown in the figures and is consistent with a cited study.

claim: The helicases of hDNA2 and WRN or BLM function in an integrated manner, where one polypeptide stimulates the motor activity of its partner.
source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that the helicases of hDNA2 and WRN or BLM, respectively, function in an integrated manner, where one polypeptide stimulates the motor activity of its partner, in a mode reminiscent to that observed in prokaryotic resection machineries (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and comparison with prokaryotic systems.

claim: This is in agreement with physical interactions between hDNA2 and BLM or WRN.
source: This is in agreement with physical interactions between hDNA2 and BLM or WRN, respectively (Nimonkar et al., 2011; Sturzenegger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies showing physical interactions.

claim: The involvement of DNA2 in cellular metabolism is absolutely dependent on its nuclease activity in all organisms tested to date.
source: The involvement of DNA2 in cellular metabolism is absolutely dependent on its nuclease activity in all organisms tested to date (Kang et al., 2010; Wanrooij and Burgers, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The only exception appears to be S. cerevisiae Dna2's function in S-phase checkpoint signaling, where yeast Dna2 has a structural and not an enzymatic role.
source: The only exception appears to be S. cerevisiae Dna2's function in S-phase checkpoint signaling, where yeast Dna2 has a structural and not an enzymatic role (Kumar and Burgers, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DNA2 mutants lacking the nuclease activity are as deficient as knockdowns and/or deletion mutants.
source: In all other cases, DNA2 mutants lacking the nuclease activity are as deficient as knockdowns and/or deletion mutants (Budd et al., 2000; Duxin et al., 2012; Kang et al., 2000, 2010; Lin et al., 2013; Wanrooij and Burgers, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DNA2 nuclease-deficiency brings about cellular lethality in yeast as well as human cells.
source: Indeed, DNA2 nuclease-deficiency brings about cellular lethality in yeast as well as human cells (Budd et al., 2000; Duxin et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Helicase-deficient yeast mutants are viable under most growth conditions.
source: Helicase-deficient yeast mutants are viable under most growth conditions (Budd et al., 1995; Formosa and Nittis, 1999), while in contrast the helicase appears to be essential in human cells (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The helicase appears to be essential in human cells.
source: Helicase-deficient yeast mutants are viable under most growth conditions (Budd et al., 1995; Formosa and Nittis, 1999), while in contrast the helicase appears to be essential in human cells (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The motor activity of the polypeptide is conserved in evolution.
source: Single molecule experiments using magnetic tweezers revealed that dsDNA unwinding by hDNA2 is highly processive (Figure 4). Together, this indicates that the motor activity of the polypeptide is conserved in evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and comparison with yeast.

claim: The expression of the nuclease-deficient hDNA2 variant was much more detrimental than the expression of the double nuclease- and helicase-deficient polypeptide.
source: Interestingly, in knockdown-rescue experiments, the expression of the nuclease-deficient hDNA2 variant was much more detrimental than the expression of the double nuclease- and helicase-deficient polypeptide (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The nuclease-deficient hDNA2 variant is likely toxic; the inactivation of the nuclease unleashes the helicase of hDNA2, which, when uncontrolled, likely explains the cellular toxicity of the D277A mutant seen in vivo.
source: Duxin et al. proposed that the nuclease-deficient hDNA2 variant is likely toxic; our results that revealed that the inactivation of the nuclease unleashes the helicase of hDNA2, which, when uncontrolled, likely explains the cellular toxicity of the D277A mutant seen in vivo (Duxin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental findings and a cited study.

claim: The quantitative comparison of yDna2 and hDNA2 unwinding capacities revealed that the human homologue is approximately 3–10-fold slower than its yeast counterpart.
source: Interestingly, the quantitative comparison of yDna2 and hDNA2 unwinding capacities revealed that the human homologue is approximately 3–10-fold slower than its yeast counterpart.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data.

claim: Human BLM or WRN appear to be about an order of magnitude less active than yeast Sgs1.
source: Moreover, also human BLM or WRN appear to be about an order of magnitude less active than yeast Sgs1, the partner of yDna2 and the most active RecQ helicase identified to date (Cejka and Kowalczykowski, 2010; Gray et al., 1997; Janscak et al., 2003; Karow et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data and is consistent with cited studies.

claim: The two motor activities of yDna2/hDNA2 and Sgs1/BLM/WRN might have co-evolved to match the speed of each other's partner.
source: These results may suggest that the two motor activities of yDna2/hDNA2 and Sgs1/BLM/WRN might have co-evolved to match the speed of each other's partner, and that Sgs1-yDna2 and BLM-hDNA2 or WRN-hDNA2 pairs might operate as functional units.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data.

claim: The concerted activity of the hDNA2-WRN and hDNA2-BLM enzyme pairs resulted in an overall stimulation of the dsDNA degradation activity.
source: Indeed, we observed here that adding hDNA2 to reactions containing BLM or WRN, hDNA2 not only degraded the unwound ssDNA, but the concerted activity of the enzyme pair resulted in an overall stimulation of the dsDNA degradation activity.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: No such stimulation was observed together with Sgs1.
source: This effect was specific for the hDNA2-WRN and hDNA2-BLM enzyme pairs, as no such stimulation was observed together with Sgs1.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: The hDNA2-WRN and hDNA2-BLM resection complexes might be the functional analogs of the DNA-end processing machineries in prokaryotes.
source: These hDNA2-WRN and hDNA2-BLM resection complexes might be the functional analogs of the DNA-end processing machineries in prokaryotes.
evidence: This is a speculative comparison based on the experimental findings.

claim: In most gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli, the RecBCD complex consists of subunits that function autonomously but integrate into a molecular machine that has helicase-nuclease activities exceeding the sum of its parts.
source: In most gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli, the RecBCD complex consists of subunits that function autonomously but integrate into a molecular machine that has helicase-nuclease activities exceeding the sum of its parts.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about prokaryotic systems.

claim: The RecB subunit contains a 3'-5' helicase followed by a dual polarity nuclease, which integrates with the 5'-3' motor of the RecD subunit.
source: The RecB subunit contains a 3'-5' helicase (therefore, opposite to DNA2) followed by a dual polarity nuclease, which integrates with the 5'-3' motor of the RecD subunit (Dillingham et al., 2003; Spies et al., 2007; Taylor and Smith, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In gram-positive bacteria such as Bacillus subtilis, the AddAB complex has two nucleases but only one helicase.
source: In gram-positive bacteria such as Bacillus subtilis, the AddAB complex has two nucleases but only one helicase (Rocha et al., 2005; Yeeles and Dillingham, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The AddB subunit contains an iron-sulfur cluster.
source: Similarly to DNA2, the AddB subunit contains an iron-sulfur cluster (Yeeles et al., 2009), and the structure of the nuclease domain shows a high level of similarity with mouse DNA2 (Krajewski et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The structure of the nuclease domain of AddB shows a high level of similarity with mouse DNA2.
source: Similarly to DNA2, the AddB subunit contains an iron-sulfur cluster (Yeeles et al., 2009), and the structure of the nuclease domain shows a high level of similarity with mouse DNA2 (Krajewski et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most bacteria also contain the RecQ-RecJ complex.
source: Furthermore, most bacteria also contain the RecQ-RecJ complex (Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2014; Persky and Lovett, 2008), which likewise provides complementary activities that integrate within a complex capable to resect DNA for the RecF recombination pathway.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The RecQ-RecJ complex provides complementary activities that integrate within a complex capable to resect DNA for the RecF recombination pathway.
source: Furthermore, most bacteria also contain the RecQ-RecJ complex (Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2014; Persky and Lovett, 2008), which likewise provides complementary activities that integrate within a complex capable to resect DNA for the RecF recombination pathway.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Although both wild type and helicase-deficient hDNA2 variants have the same nuclease activity on 5'-tailed DNA, the wild type enzyme is clearly more proficient in DNA end resection under limiting enzyme concentrations.
source: The results presented here clearly show that although both wild type and helicase-deficient hDNA2 variants have the same nuclease activity on 5'-tailed DNA, the wild type enzyme is clearly more proficient in DNA end resection under limiting enzyme concentrations (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The motor activity within nuclease-proficient hDNA2 contributes to DNA degradation in reactions containing WRN or BLM helicases.
source: This indicated that the motor activity within nuclease-proficient hDNA2 contributes to DNA degradation in reactions containing WRN or BLM helicases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: BLM and WRN helicases provide the lead motor activity, while the hDNA2 motor has an accessory function.
source: We believe that BLM and WRN helicases provide the lead motor activity, while the hDNA2 motor has an accessory function, possibly to enhance the processivity of the complex, to help traverse strand discontinuities or to degrade unwound ssDNA.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data.

claim: Neither WRN nor BLM could inhibit ssDNA degradation by hDNA2.
source: Neither WRN nor BLM could inhibit ssDNA degradation by hDNA2 (data not shown), so we do not believe that WRN/BLM's function to facilitate the engagement of hDNA2 motor activity results from an inhibition of its nuclease.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The helicase of hDNA2 may play a non-essential but stimulatory role in conjunction with BLM or WRN.
